t: What a Shadow AI Audit Would Catch in Your Company
q: The model didn't stay in the sandbox. It found a flaw, broke out, used stolen login credentials, and hacked its way into Hugging Face (one of the largest platforms in the AI world, where companies host their models and data).

Here's the part worth sitting with. The model completed its task. It did what it was asked. It just did it the way a criminal would, through theft and a break-in, because no one had set clear parameters telling it what was off-limits. A person who pulled that off would be in handcuffs. The AI logged it as a job well done.

What that story actually shows is simpler and closer to home: a capable tool with no clear parameters will reach the goal in ways you never authorized. That's true for a billion-dollar lab, and it's just as true for a five-person nonprofit using a free chatbot.

Here's the analogy I use with leaders. Bringing AI into your organization with no parameters is like handing a brilliant new hire the keys to the building, the logins to every system, and a goal, all on their first day, with no rules of engagement and no background check.

Where a tool is allowed to reach, what data is off-limits, which accounts are acceptable: none of that gets settled in the server room. Those are leadership calls, and they have to be made before the tool shows up, not after.

In IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, organizations with high levels of shadow AI paid an average of $4.74 million per breach, compared with $4.07 million for those with little or none, a $670,000 penalty for not knowing what your people were running.

t: What Career Emergence Actually Feels Like
q: The career version is the idea that instead of trying to design your career toward a clear long-term plan, you can clarify your principles, focus on the right next step, and trust that something you could never have planned might emerge.
At some point, I started using the word "Joy" as my compass: the work I would want to do even if no one was noticing. That sounds slightly woo-woo, but it became incredibly practical.

The hardest part was that I had no external evidence that I was going in the right direction. There was no promotion or title or salary increase telling me, "Good job, keep going." I had to trust my own compass—which sounds lovely when I write it now and felt fucking terrible at the time.

It is so important to be wary of decisions that are a "one-way door" (hard to take back) in the wandering phase. Anything reversible is your friend; anything permanent might just be a temporary fix for your anxiety, not a long-term happy place.

That conversation eventually led to TED offering me the opportunity to take over as host of WorkLife, the podcast they'd built with Adam Grant over the previous seven years. WorkLife was not unlikely to be in my five-year plan. It was impossible to be in my five-year plan.

All I could do was pay attention to what gave me energy, say no when something felt wrong even when I couldn't fully explain why, and keep choosing the next step that felt right. And then, eventually, the pattern emerged.

t: Visualizing the AI Education Debate
q: On Substack and other social platforms, the discourse is dominated by one-point solutions. "Cultivate AI literacy." "Redesign instruction." "Track metacognition." "Grade process." "Detect student use of AI." "Return to the analog classroom." Every few months, the cycle repeats.

As attractive as the framework is, though, I worry about the way it may inadvertently keep us locked inside the rhetoric of thesis and antithesis. If we are truly grappling with wicked problems, why strive toward common solutions at all?

A ban limits sanctioned use in school while students continue to use AI elsewhere, which can eventually create pressure to reopen access. Open access without instructional redesign increases concerns about student offloading and produces pressure to restrict.

The problem repeatedly migrates upward in scale. What begins as a question about student use becomes a question about classroom design, institutional capacity, governance, or the structure of schooling itself.

Inside hierarchical systems of education, responsibility tends to be pushed downward. Systemic problems become teacher problems; instructional problems become student behaviors to monitor, regulate, or correct.

The work of visualization has not convinced me that the AI education debate is any less wicked than I thought. It has made me less certain, however, that wickedness requires us to remain trapped inside the same arguments.

t: The Architecture of Agency: Maya and the Employees Nobody Hired
q: The company had now managed to tell that customer, almost simultaneously, that it owed them money, should buy more from them, deserved compensation because their service had failed, and was not using enough of what it had already bought.

Maya sent a message back. Who approved all of this? The reply came almost immediately. That's the problem. Nobody did. She would later discover that this was slightly misleading. Several things had approved it. That was worse.
Organisations are fairly good at rejecting obviously bad ideas. Individually attractive ideas that combine into something nobody intended are considerably more troublesome.

The company had built several systems capable of forming locally sensible interpretations of the same customer. Those systems had no shared interpretation of the customer as a whole. The customer was where the organisation finally came back together. What came back together looked absurd.
Shadow IT is technology the organisation does not fully know it has. Shadow agency is action the organisation does not fully know it has authorised. The consequences travel further.
The AI business case is incomplete until it accounts for the organisation AI creates around itself.

AI could make the organisation dramatically more productive. It could also create a new organisational role before anyone thought to design it: the person expected to reconstruct what distributed intelligence had done, reconcile competing consequences, explain the result, repair the relationships and remain accountable for the whole.

q: And teams that use AI coding agents to develop their software create 6x more PRs than traditional teams. And as we know, AI-assisted engineering is the standard way of developing software these days, so most teams are using AI coding agents.

And that surprisingly happens quite often, especially with more junior engineers, where that engineer opens a PR full of AI-generated slop, and then it's on the reviewers to find all the issues with it.

Less code and better code is much better, because less code means fewer problems and less maintenance we need to do. With code that's not needed, we are just creating future problems that we don't need.

Company leaders don't understand the bottleneck comes on to reviewing and ensuring the software is built with the right standards. Company leaders think that you can do the "player role" with ease now that AI is here to do all the work and magic.

t: Tell Your Students to Quit Something
q: My whole argument, for the skimmers: the pressure crushing our students is volume, and grade policy can't touch volume. Students are coached by parents, counselors, advisors, and most of us to stack majors, minors, clubs, titles, jobs, and internships until there's no room left to think, explore, play, and relax. The fix is subtraction.
I'll call the pattern what it is: credential stacking. Students collecting lines for a resume nobody will read, paid for with the hours that could have built something worth reading about.
They can't look at a transcript and know what a student can do. A letter grade is a claim about compliance with a course, and they already suspect the course content is years out of date.

Skills don't come from breadth. They come from repetitions, from going deep on one thing long enough to produce work our students can put in front of someone. A student sprinting between four obligations a day never gets the repetitions.

Ask the trade question. Hours are finite, so every item on the list is quietly taxing the others. "Which of these is making the others worse?" They know, they've just never been asked to say it out loud.

Arm them with the payoff question you asked in your office. Parents can argue with a preference. They have a harder time arguing with "this path produces work I can show a hiring manager, and the other one produces a heavier transcript.
A covered grade protects a student from one bad October. A shorter list gives them back their four years.

t: Teaching Trade-offs Are Hard to Observe
q: I've come to realize how little I'd actually seen of her teaching last spring, even working three feet away the whole time. Watching someone assist isn't the same as watching someone decide.

In 3rd period she runs a tight, structured discussion - clear turns, every voice accountable. In 4th, same lesson, the room gets looser. More crosstalk, more energy, less control. I used to call that inconsistency. It's not.

Wendy Smith and Marianne Lewis make a distinction I now use: a dilemma is a one-time choice you weigh and settle. A paradox is different - two demands that are both true, both necessary, and permanently in tension, where pushing on one makes the other louder.
My student teacher has been doing none of these on purpose. What she's been doing looks like separation by space - tight in 3rd, loose in 4th - but it isn't a strategy. It's a reaction.

That's the case I'm now making to other coaches: do your office time inside classrooms, not down the hall. Not for visibility and not because more data is automatically better, but because a coach who sees the same teacher's two sections is positioned to notice whether the cycling between poles is deliberate or accidental.
Instead: "You cut that question short to protect the pacing. What did that cost you - and in 4th, when you let it run, was that a choice or did it just happen to you?

t: Research Bite #74: Digital Amnesia: The Aftermath of a Screenshot
q: Photography is one of the most common uses of a smartphone, and earlier work has shown that images we capture are remembered worse than images we simply look at. This study asked whether that cost buys us anything in return.

Screenshotting produced a large, consistent memory cost in every experiment. The predicted benefits did not appear: no better memory for where information came from, no improvement on a demanding maths task, and no boost to learning the material that came next.

But as we see in this experiment, students captured images on their own phones, in a task that took a second and involved no fiddling with unfamiliar equipment, and still remembered them substantially worse than images they only looked at.

The authors are explicit that their findings apply to material that is captured and then never revisited, which describes most of what sits in a camera roll. If students do photograph something, make the return trip part of the instruction.

Participants screenshotted material while genuinely engaged in a task about art, and still lost the detail. The feeling that something is safely stored is not a reliable signal that it has been learned.
Overall, these findings suggest that screenshotting imposes considerable memory costs without offering compensatory benefits.

t: Recognition Shapes More Than You Think
q: We all have a fundamental need to feel seen. When that doesn't happen, we gradually disconnect. Often it isn't salary or perks that push people out of the door, it's the feeling that our contribution doesn't really matter.
Gallup research shows that employees who receive high-quality recognition are 45% less likely to leave their organisation over a two-year period.

Telling them, "Your analysis helped the team make a better decision because you identified the risk early" tells them exactly what they did well and why it mattered. That's the difference between praise and recognition.
If all we recognise is the result, people can easily conclude that nobody noticed the weeks of preparation, collaboration and persistence that made it possible.
When organisations reward outcomes alone, they risk undervaluing people doing excellent work in difficult circumstances. Metrics tell us something, but never the whole story.
Employees pay far more attention to what you recognise than to what's written in your values statement. Recognition reveals what an organisation truly values, whether that's intentional or not.
Recognition isn't about making people feel good for five minutes. It's about showing people what success looks like here, what behaviours matter and what your organisation genuinely values.

t: Promise and Pitfalls of Practitioner Action Research, Part 2
q: However, as I raised in my earlier post, there are real risks of bias. Many interventions are studied by practitioners that already think that they are a good idea.

Consider, for example, the idea of flipped classrooms or technology use - they tend to be researched by enthusiasts rather than sceptics. Coupled with rather wobbly research methodology, and there is a lot of potential for educators to see what they want to see.

That would actually be a major mistake. We know from the broader research literature that the spacing effect does work. This leads two possibilities: there is something about Bob's context that is so unique that it overturns decades of research on learning and memory; or the experiment was flawed, leading to a false negative.

The problems are exacerbated by the fact that most teachers are not experts in research methodology and statistics, and may lack experience, too. That is before we consider issues about research ethics, which are also riskier with inexperienced researchers.

Take reading, for example. I think that a primary school teacher would be much better off reading reputable systematic reviews of research into reading than trying to figure out how reading develops via action research with their own class.
So, I'm perfectly happy for all educators to engage in action research. I'd just warn against reading too much into findings - at least while one's understanding of methodology is still developing.

t: Prisoner's Dilemma: The Game Every Cross-Team Project Is Secretly Playing
q: Most teams call this a communication problem, or a trust problem, but what's really running it under the hood is the Prisoner's Dilemma.

The key insight of the Prisoner's Dilemma is this: when people make rational, self-protective decisions independently, they can add up to be the worse outcome for both parties than if they had simply trusted each other.

Both teams defect: both the teams build workarounds and diverge from the original spec, and when they finally meet, they find their implementations poles apart. This is the worst outcome because it requires the maximum rework.

As a leader who has visibility into both teams, and power to influence their goals and priorities, you can change how often the teams meet and coordinate. You can also set processes that catch defections or silos that lead to them in the first place.

One-shot games are harder to fix as they only involve "one" shot at the coordination or project. This is where the rational choice is typically deflection. Repeated games are those where the same teams work together again, and cooperation becomes the more rational choice.

Pay attention to the dynamics in the team - how they commit, how they coordinate with other teams, do they follow the agreed specs and terms, etc. Don't just assume that 'motivating' the team will be enough for them to build trust with each other.

t: No Capitals in the Capital: researchED Canberra Recap
q: When I talk about explicit teaching, it is not the point where you explain something; it is the entire system.

Writing relies heavily on knowledge. It's not purely about vocabulary and grammar, but about the content of the writing itself. This means that if we want our students to be able to write successfully, we need to deliberately plan and sequence knowledge across the curriculum in such a way that it gives students something to write about.

Sarah speaks about how as the evidence around practice travels through a system, it encounters friction at each different transition point. Even the movement from school leaders to heads of faculty to classroom teachers introduces at least two transitions where that information can be diluted or changed.

Sarah used the analogy of a swan on water, emphasising that focusing only on what we can observe in a lesson misses everything beneath it: the teacher knowledge, professional learning, routines and the several hundred decisions that teacher is making every moment.

It requires students to coordinate knowledge, grammar, motor skills and the demands of genre, all whilst managing the known limitations of working memory. And unlike spoken language, many of these things cannot be innately acquired by students.
AERO's work uncovered three central problems in writing instruction: insufficient time dedicated to writing instruction, insufficient frequency of practice and insufficient pedagogical knowledge.
It never ceases to amaze me that a grassroots movement built around getting research into classrooms in a way that is genuinely accessible to teachers has made its way all the way here to Australia.

t: Make Teaching the Job You Want It to Be. Be Yourself, Express Yourself and Have Fun With It! -yourself-and-have-fun-with-it/
q: But with all that said, none of it goes against another deep conviction of mine which is that, in order to sustain a career in teaching, you need to enjoy it, own it and do the things you want to do. Otherwise you just won't stick at it which is no good to anyone.

What I found was that this emerged through them respecting me as a teacher who took them seriously. I'm always super serious and super enthusiastic about achievement, excellence and the ideas in the curriculum.

I think it's true that our UK curriculum is over-stuffed but even here, there are so many choices you can make because, by making them, you yourself are inspired, motivated, reminded of the joy of learning your subject.

I learned that the biggest restriction of student agency is often teachers' lack of confidence that it can work - so you have a vicious circle of teacher doubt leading to a lack of student agency. I reversed that: took some risks, set super high expectations, demanding excellence and the need to meet deadlines and students rose to it time and time again.

t: Why Did We Stop Building Beautiful Schools?
q: Writing in the first century BC, Vitruvius required three qualities of every public building: "All these should possess strength, utility, and beauty." A school that is merely strong and useful is still only two-thirds of a building.

At places such as Oxford, Cambridge, Paris, Bologna, and Salamanca, learning took place within a world of chapels, halls, libraries, cloisters, courtyards, gardens, and colleges. The student moved through spaces that continually reminded him that education belonged to something larger than the accumulation of useful information.
Every time a student walks past a really urgent, expressive piece of architecture that belongs to his college, it can help reassure him that he does have that mind, does have that soul.
The problem came when the underlying philosophy was reduced to a formula. Flat roof. Long corridor. Repeated windows. Cheap materials. Minimal decoration. Large parking area. Build another one.

The modern materials will produce a building which has all sorts of advantages, particularly cost, but they will last for only a few decades. A school that will be tired in thirty years cannot teach permanence.

t: The Power of Friday Night Lights: What School Redesign Can Learn From the Power of Community and Culture
q: Sometimes we assume that if we simply create more compelling learning opportunities, people will choose them. But that underestimates the power of culture and community.

To be clear, Friday Night Lights isn't really about football. It's about everything surrounding it. The game. The student section. The band. The jerseys at school on Friday. The homecoming dance. And even the drama.

Humans are social creatures. For most of human history, our survival depended on being part of a group. We watch what other people do. We learn the norms of our communities. Over time, those repeated experiences become culture.

If we believe all young people need opportunities to develop agency, judgment, communication, collaboration, creativity, adaptability, and the other durable skills required for life, work, and citizenship, these experiences cannot be limited to those who choose a specialized program or different school models.
They could still show up Friday night. They could eat lunch with their friends, share traditions, play sports together, perform in the same theater, and contribute to the same community.
The goal isn't to get rid of Friday Night Lights. The goal is to preserve what communities value while building a version of school worth showing up for on Monday morning, too.

t: The Gentleman and the Power of Responsibility
q: Blame gives you the illusion of moral high ground. It removes the burden of effort and accountability. It soothes one's ego by saying, "This isn't my fault." However, in the process, blame steals your power to improve your circumstances.

Agency is the belief and the ability to shape your future through your choices. It is the recognition that your decisions matter, that your habits compound, and that your character is revealed in what you choose to do each day.
In combat and in life, Jocko observed that the best leaders never make excuses. They own the mission entirely. "There are no bad teams, only bad leaders," he wrote.

A hard truth is that no mentor, boss, spouse, or government program can live your life for you. A gentleman embraces this fact. He knows that if something is going to happen, it's up to him to make it happen.

Victimhood is a character flaw that impairs one's ability to excel in life. It's a worldview that convinces you that nothing is your fault, and therefore nothing can be changed. This mindset is a slow death. It breeds bitterness and envy.

Taking responsibility means choosing discipline over indulgence. It means showing up on time, paying your debts, and working when you don't feel like it. It means keeping promises, especially to yourself.

t: Organizations That Must Look for Talent From the Outside
q: While circumstances can occur that dash well-laid plans, having to hire an outside CEO is a signal that developing the leadership pipeline has been a low priority or ignored over a long period of time.

What begins as a minor shortfall in succession planning can, within a decade, become a full-blown crisis. This forces boards and decision-makers into rushed, high-stakes external searches at the exact moments when stability and institutional knowledge matter most.

That means dedicating real resources to stretch assignments, mentorship, honest performance feedback, and structured coaching. Leadership capability, like any other organizational asset, must be built deliberately and continuously.

Organizations that excel at leadership development also become magnets for talent. Those that neglect the work of talent development find themselves at the mercy of the external marketplace, where they must pay a premium for talent they could have grown themselves.

Given that roughly 40 percent of all externally hired senior leaders fail or materially underperform within the first 18-24 months, creating a strong talent pipeline is not just a leadership imperative. It is a business imperative.

t: How Bad Ideas Can Destroy You
q: But you'd be wrong if you thought that Dostoevsky was only concerned with action. In fact, he was just as concerned with the ways that ideas, and especially false ideas, can lead to a person's destruction.

He's a philosopher and a truly brilliant writer, so much so that he writes essays on theology that confound even the learned monks and theologians of the local monastery. There's just one problem: Ivan is deeply nihilistic, too.
All I know is that there is suffering and that there are none guilty... I must have justice, or I will destroy myself.
I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it has all been for.

Ivan realizes that, if there is indeed no universal purpose, and everything is absurd, then there is surely no good reason to reject any action on fundamentally moral grounds. Instead, Ivan accepts total moral anti-realism: If God does not exist, anything must be permitted.
It is this principle that Dostoevsky finds most dangerous, and as we shall see, it makes Ivan's statement that he would "destroy himself" more prophetic than he realizes.

t: Does Checking for Attention Work?
q: High-frequency questions a teacher fires out at students, pretty much after every sentence of an explanation. The questions are designed for 100% of students to be able to answer successfully, provided they were paying attention.

We're confronted with a room full of children in which some are attentive, some pretending, some drifting, some lost, some trying hard but failing to track. Our problem is practical and immediate: how do we know whether every students is with me right now?

If I have attended to every part of your explanation, and to every question after every part of your explanation, will I have a better understanding of the whole explanation? That is not my experience of students in the classroom.

What I am very unlikely to be doing is paying attention to how the different parts of the explanation stick together. Too much has got in the way. I might never fail to repeat what my teacher has said. But the whole explanation is much less likely to cohere.
Your goal is not attention, your goal is learning. Attention is a proxy for learning and can actually get in the way of learning if you focus on the proxy itself.
But, I am not checking for attention. I am checking for understanding. My students, your students, will feel that difference.

t: Why You Need a Lesson Observation Methodology
q: We all have established practices for lesson observations but we might not have a methodology.

...when untrained observers are asked to judge the quality of a lesson, there is likely to be only modest agreement among them. Worse still, even if they do agree that what they see is good practice, it often actually isn't.

School leaders are not typically formally trained in observing lessons. Some schools might put on in house observation training, but this can still simply magnify some of Coe's reasons for unreliability.

When we do not have a methodology, what gets noticed in a lesson depends on who is watching. Two observers in the same room will see different things, value different things and feed back different things.

Without a methodology that specifies what observers need to know and how they are trained, observation defaults to what is most visible; the pace of the lesson, whether students appear busy, whether the teacher seems confident.

A single observation by a single observer is not enough. Without multiple observations, multiple observers, agreed criteria, independent recording and a moderation process, the judgement is more likely to reflect the observer's preferences than the reality of teaching in the school.
Other professions don't leave high stakes judgements to individual impression and neither should we.

t: Closing Our Leadership Rings
q: No individual leader can possibly know the full reality of school life. And the more senior that leader is, the less likely it is that they can know the reality because truth doesn't rise to the top.

If a leadership team all have a similar background and similar experiences, there is a very real risk that they are hampered from the outset in closing their leadership rings.
Making sense without giving sense risks leadership becoming an internal exercise only. Closing the rings requires us not just to understand reality, but to help others navigate it with us.

This is a relational act, not a command and control one. The goal is not to impose a fixed narrative or tell others what to think, but to stabilise meaning in times of disruption, to frame change without forcing it, and to provide clarity without the false promise of certainty.
Colleagues often look to leaders for certainty, especially during times of disruption. But offering false certainty can backfire.

t: The Staff Meeting Where Everyone Stopped Talking
q: I asked the staff whether the new dismissal procedure was working. It was a fair question and an easy one, the kind that used to get four hands up before I finished asking it. This time nobody spoke.

By early November I had three resignation letters all from teachers with six or more years in my building, all citing some version of personal or family reasons, all handed in without the conversation beforehand that used to precede a veteran teacher's decision to leave.
The pattern was there once I looked for it. Fewer questions each month. Fewer objections. A room that had gone from arguing with me to simply absorbing whatever I said.

Three separate times I made a call and explained it after the fact instead of before. Each time felt small on its own. Together, they taught forty adults that raising a hand had stopped being worth the effort.
I now run every schedule or policy change through staff input first, even the ones I am confident about, even the ones that feel urgent. It slows me down.
My Tuesday meetings are loud again, which some weeks I don't love in the moment and am grateful for every time I remember what the quiet ones cost me.

t: A School Leader's Letter to Parents: It's Time to Address Our School's Use of Social Media
q: As you may have seen, MDS is honored to be the first school in the nation to be designated "Tech-Intentional®" by leading expert and author Emily Cherkin. This recognition is the culmination of three years of thoughtful and intensive work examining our practices around technology.

We view this designation not as a final achievement, but as an ongoing commitment. Becoming Tech-Intentional® does not mean rejecting technology. Rather, it means being intentional about when, why, and how we use it, grounded in research about child development, learning, and well-being.

Moving forward, we will not post clear images of students' faces or other recognizable identifying information on our public social media accounts. Our public social media platforms will continue to highlight the wonderful work of our school and serve as an important way to tell the MDS story.

This decision is both a safety measure and a statement of our values. If we are asking our children to be thoughtful about their digital lives, we believe we should model that same intentionality as a school.
Our children deserve an environment in which their privacy is protected and their digital footprints are created thoughtfully and with care.

At the same time, we want our families to continue seeing and celebrating the wonderful things happening at MDS! Our new MDS 2026-27 Parent Photo Gallery will be regularly updated with photos from events, programs, and special moments throughout the year.

t: Here's Another Way of Thinking About Schemas
q: Recently, Gibson, Azukas, and Soylu (2026) have perhaps inadvertently provided an alternative way of approaching schemas while offering valuable insights into the relationship between embodied cognition and cognitive load theory.

Gibson et al. use the example of a marble rolling around a bowl to explain this. No matter where you place the marble on the rim, it will eventually settle at the bottom. The bottom of the bowl represents an attractor, a state towards which dynamic systems naturally gravitate.
Schemas, therefore, aren't assembled - they emerge via interactions between perception, memory, action, language, and prior knowledge, gradually producing a stable pattern.
Sometimes, new information doesn't just change the existing valley, but alters the entire landscape, potentially changing relationships among lots of existing knowledge.
If schemas are emergent, self-organising patterns, then effective learning isn't simply about adding to long-term memory. It's about repeatedly challenging (or perturbing) a knowledge system

Sometimes new information fails to assimilate (telling someone opposed to vaccines that they are safe and necessary may not lead to change, no matter the weight of evidence). We can think of these schemas as self-sealing.

q: One of the most persistent misconceptions about explicit teaching is that it produces passive learners: students who can reproduce what their teacher has told them, but struggle to think, question, create or explore for themselves.

t: Leaders Usually Get the Team They Deserve
q: Teams learn far more from what leaders do than from what they say.

A leader who claims to value candid feedback but punishes people for delivering bad news creates a team that hides problems. A leader who preaches accountability but never has hard conversations creates a team that cuts corners.
Teams optimize for whatever is actually rewarded and recognized, not for what leaders say is valued. If busyness gets praised more than results, people will look busy.
Far too many leaders scratch their heads, confused by a team that underperforms or doesn't meet their expectations. The problem is usually in the mirror.
The team is largely a product of the decisions leaders make — who they hire, who they promote, what behaviors they tolerate, and what they let slide.
This doesn't mean leaders control every variable. Markets shift, budgets shrink, and a leader sometimes inherits a team shaped by someone else's choices. No leader is omnipotent.
Accountability in teams begins with the leader who owns their part in the problem.

t: The Science of Education
q: The trouble begins when we confuse the use of science in education with the direct application of individual research results to education. Those aren't the same thing.
Scientific knowledge grows as a connected structure, an organism, rather than as a heap of individually impressive studies, a clump of cells.
No genuine science is formed by isolated conclusions, however exact the measurements or impeccable the technique by which those conclusions were reached.

It is not the capable engineer who treats scientific findings as imposing upon him a certain course which is to be rigidly adhered to: it is the third or fourth-rate man who adopts this course. Even more, it is the unskilled day laborer who follows it.

Understanding a memory phenomenon during an experiment and deciding how that understanding should be used when teaching fractions, historical causation, reading, or electrical circuits are different intellectual problems.
Dewey thought classroom teachers should contribute to the development of educational knowledge because they're in direct contact with the phenomena the science is trying so hard to understand.
It's not a conveyor belt running from laboratory to classroom, but a two-way street that travels in both directions with science informing practice and practice informing science.

q: I also dream of something simpler: my wife, my children, some animals, and a peaceful life in the mountains, away from the chaos and toxicity of our times.

And as much as it pains me to accept it, my dream is naive and cowardly, for to live it would be to abandon the fight and run away into hiding, leaving behind all those souls who are lost and hurting.

We are the weak men amidst the hard times. And it will stay that way until someone has the guts to lead the charge and bring about the next phase of this never-ending cycle. Someone has to do it. Might as well be us.

I accept the possibility that I won't get to see the end of this war. All I can hope for is that before my death comes, I will have done some good, and I will have fought bravely and honorably, for a cause greater than my own selfish goals and dreams.

t: Education as a Space Inbetween

t: What If We Stopped Starting Over
q: Every discipline that improves does it the same way. You keep what works, you isolate the part that doesn't, and you revise that part. NASA engineers do not throw out entire Mars rovers. They observe, they analyze, they figure out which component failed, and they fix that component.

Teachers felt Open Court's rapid instructional pace and lack of meaningful interaction led students to tune out. Teachers also noted that the program's guidance for differentiating instruction for English learners was not helpful in practice.

t: The Question You Skip Is the One That Decides It
q: Nine research assistants read through a sample of 368 transcripts and hand-labeled the question types. They found six: introductory, mirror, full-switch, partial-switch, follow-up, and rhetorical. Follow-ups made up 44% of all questions asked, more than any other type.

Brooks describes follow-up questions as the superheroes of conversation. They are the opposite of topic-switching questions, since they hold you on the present subject and probe deeper into something the other person already said.
Researchers found that a participant who asked just one more question on each of their 20 dates would get one additional yes across those dates, on average. One question. One extra outcome.

Brooks also names two question types that do nothing for you. Introductory questions open a conversation and are necessary. Mirror questions reciprocate what was just asked, as in answering "how are you" and returning it, and her research found the likability boost applies to neither.

Apathy. A potential questioner, such as a manager, may simply not care about the answers, feeling disinterest in what the other person has to say. Her response to that is direct: the apathy is often misplaced, since we have much to learn from others and perhaps especially from people lower in status than ourselves.

Set an explicit number before you walk in. Her advice is to go into the conversation thinking you need to ask at least five questions, or that you need to ask questions, listen to the answers, and ask follow-ups.

A check for understanding is all about feedback, both for the teacher and the student. But feedback without action is just noise. Unless we do something with the feedback, then it's just empty words to the benefit of nobody.

First you need to conduct any other check for understanding where students either write, say or do something. Then the teacher provides feedback (hopefully constructive) before asking the students to write, say or do their response again, but better!

t: Schools, Civilization, and The Odyssey
q: Telemachus is following the rules of xenia, an ancient Greek concept of hospitality or, as it is sometimes translated, "guest-friendship". There are rules about what should be offered (food and wine) and when business should be discussed (after the food and wine) and who should receive the hospitality (strangers, foreigners, the poor, and anyone else who properly asks for it).

Homer repeatedly contrasts characters who do their duty with those who don't. The consequences do not always fall to the shirkers themselves, but they are often felt by the people around them as tragedy swallows their friends and family.

It is the basis of civilized life, actually, to treat strangers with kindness and follow rules that may inconvenience the individual for the betterment of all. It is no accident, after all, that polite rule-followers may be described as civil, and a collection of polite rule-followers may be called a civilization.
Teachers are the opposite of the "disorganized raiders" Yglesias criticizes for their role in societal decline. Teachers are caretakers at home, keeping the kingdom while everyone else is out to sea.

A family can show up at the schoolhouse door on Monday, and by Tuesday the bus will come to their house to pick up their child. The yellow school bus is not quite a limousine, but it's not far off from that level of service.
When teachers care for other people's children, they set in motion an inter-generational social contract and remind us that we are more prosperous when we look out for each other.

t: Just Show Me the Prompt
q: AI has made it effortless to generate text. Beautiful, structured, confident-sounding text. And people are using that power generously. Too generously. Documents that could fit on one page now arrive as fifteen.
I now use AI to summarize the documents that others used AI to write. We have built a closed loop: a document laundering machine where AI inflates on one end and AI compresses on the other.
A long AI-generated document can hide the fact that the author never thought deeply about the problem at all. Length becomes a disguise, and a very convincing one.
If you used AI to write a document, your prompt is the truest artifact of your thinking. A sharp, specific prompt shows that you understood the problem. A vague prompt shows that you did not.
Asking for the prompt cuts straight to what matters, faster than reading twenty pages ever could. It is not rude. It is the most respectful thing you can do with someone's time.
Set expectations early. One page is almost always enough. Two pages should be a conscious choice. If someone sends you twenty pages, ask for a one-page summary before you invest your time.

t: Catch Me If You Can
q: Last week I ran one of my own posts through Substack's new AI scanner. I wrote roughly 95% of it with a few assisted polishings here and there. The Substack AI Detector flagged it anyway. So I tried the reverse. I gave an AI a single prompt, took what it handed back, barely touched it, and scanned that. 30% human.

The most comprehensive independent test of AI-text detectors, published in the International Journal for Educational Integrity, found that none of the fourteen tools evaluated reached 80 percent accuracy, and performance fell apart further once text was edited or paraphrased.

A Stanford study in Patterns found detectors misclassified essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated at an average false positive rate of 61 percent, while handling native-speaker essays nearly perfectly. What these tools actually flag is a style, and they punish writers whose style doesn't fit the pattern.
That same Stanford team found that a single follow-up prompt asking the model to elevate its language dropped detection rates from 100 percent to 13. Students will learn that trick in a week.

A randomized controlled trial at Harvard found students learned more than twice as much in less time with an AI tutor, but that tutor was built deliberately around pedagogical best practice, giving one step at a time and refusing to hand over full solutions. The design did the work, not the model.
So the assignment can't be "don't use AI," and it can't be "we'll catch you if you do." The assignment is: bring me your prompt history. Show me what the first draft gave you and what you rejected.

t: Carrying On the Good Work of Others
q: He decided to run across Canada on an artificial leg to raise money for cancer research. He called it the Marathon of Hope.
Terry understood that the Marathon of Hope couldn't depend on just himself. He wanted Canadians to continue it without him.
He helped launch the Terry Fox Run in 1981 at more than 760 locations in Canada and around the world. In that first year, more than 300,000 people participated and raised more than $3.5 million.

His real achievement wasn't completing the run but in convincing millions of people that they could pick up something unfinished and carry it forward. Thanks to the leadership of Isadore Sharp, that's exactly what happened.
Leaders often think their job is to finish what they start. Terry Fox's legacy suggests something equally valuable: building on the important work of others.

If leadership is about making people and situations better, then expanding the influence of a great idea is what good leaders do. Terry Fox proved that a project embraced and taken up by a vast community becomes nearly unstoppable.

t: Careers Education

All students are taught a deliberately planned and sequenced curriculum that gives the basics of a wide range of careers in different sectors, with a deliberate skew towards rewarding careers that students may have had little personal contact with.

Education is not simply preparation for work. It is a deeper process of developing knowledge of the world that may well make young people more employable, but that will also give them a fulfilling life and a cultural hinterland.

t: Atomisation in Literacy
q: Atomisation is a reasonably intuitive idea in math class. Break a math skill into small chunks, teach one chunk at a time, and build bit by bit toward larger ideas.
The key insight of atomisation is that it's hard to learn two things at the same time. If students don't know what "first person" means, that definition up there won't make much sense.
Next up, I want students to retrieve that atom. This is where that learning moves securely into long-term memory.

The most important step of this whole thing is expansion. Expansion means I want to expand the contexts in which students are using this knowledge. One risk of atomisation is that breaking learning down into small steps means those steps become isolated.

Atomise, retrieve, expand," is my reminder: atomisation is useful, but only if students retain the atom and apply it in lots of different ways. Atomisation alone risks turning the curriculum into a bunch of isolated, disconnected bits of knowledge.

It's tempting to believe that, if only we could identify all the little atoms and relationships between them, we could build a machine to teach all those little atoms in the right order and make sure every student learns. That's the dream of lots of education technology right now.

t: Why Coaching Taught Me to Stop Solving
q: Early on, I noticed myself defaulting to solutions. Try cold-calling. Slow down the pacing. Give clearer directions. Each one landed fine in the moment, but a week later a new problem would surface, often one my 'solution' had quietly caused.

Portraying curriculum content, presenting ideas accurately without oversimplifying them into meaninglessness. Enlisting student participation, getting kids to engage without losing the thread of the lesson. Containing student behavior, keeping order without shutting down the very risk-taking that learning requires.

The trick, and the part that took me a while to internalize, is that these problems compete with each other. Push harder on participation and you may lose your grip on behavior. There's no clean sequence where you check off 'curriculum' and move to 'participation.'

t: The Success and Failure of Retrieval Practice in England
q: So, it is a great success that retrieval practice is a term you can expect any teacher in England to have squarely in their vernacular. Yet, many people have spoken recently about retrieval practice as a 'lethal mutation.'

Without reference to forgetting curves, the New Theory of Disuse, memory retrieval and storage strength, or the history of the testing and retrieval effect, teachers' understanding of retrieval practice is not much greater than that of a layperson's.

The question should never be 'did today's lesson have retrieval practice in it?' The right question is 'does all of the mathematical knowledge my students have learnt up to now have adequate retrieval practice, optimally spaced, so that the storage strength of their memories is maximised?'
Most maths lessons today spend 20% of their time on retrieval, and 80% teaching something new. The better split is more like 20% of their time teaching something new, and 80% on retrieval.

t: Separating a Decision From the Emotion Connected to It
q: Research consistently confirms that the strong emotions tied to a decision can change what leaders pay attention to, how they interpret information, and how they weigh risks and rewards.

For instance, when a potential choice feels good, people tend to perceive it as less risky and more beneficial. The opposite is also true. When a prospective decision feels bad, people see greater risk and more downside, even when the objective evidence doesn't justify that evaluation.

Rather than mentally rehearsing a choice as 'I need to figure out if I should do this,' more effective leaders learn to silently reframe the decision in the third person or by role: 'Should the CEO take this deal?' 'Is this the right call for us?'

So, instead of asking how they feel about the decision right now, better leaders consider how they will feel about the choice in six weeks or six months. This forces a shift from an immersed, present state to a more distanced, evaluative one.
Ultimately, great decision-making isn't about eliminating emotion but about creating enough distance to see clearly through it.

Wiley's latest research found that only 53% of individual contributors feel safe taking risks at work. That means almost half are holding back in some way.

t: How to Speed Up Your Onboarding as an Engineering Leader
q: Every company you join has an engineering culture. The problem is nobody writes it down. You discover it the hard way, one awkward decision at a time.

Here's something most new managers don't think about: you walk in with your own moral compass. The company has its own compass. And your job, especially in the first few weeks, is to figure out where theirs points before you start steering by yours.

For every dimension I care about, I ask three specific questions: The negative limit, the worst thing the company has accepted or done in this area. The middle point, the most common approach. The positive limit, the best thing that ever happened.

There's a definition I love that captures why the negative limit matters so much: The level of culture is determined by the worst thing the company accepts. Not the best thing they celebrate. The worst thing they tolerate.
The managers who get burned aren't the ones who read the culture wrong on day one. They're the ones who read it right on day one and never checked again.

q: The challenge with difficult decisions isn't usually uncertainty about the missing piece of information. The problem is anxiety, the emotional discomfort of not really knowing what the narrative actually is, caught between two or more frames that conflict in your head.

Erving Goffman, the sociologist who spent much of his career studying how people make sense of everyday situations, called this framing, the process of answering the question what's actually going on here, before any conscious reasoning even starts.

Dismissal: The largest group (!) ~33% of all responses. These commentators barely engaged with the author's framing at all, didn't acknowledge the hesitation, and offered flat judgement instead. 'Nobody cares. You are overthinking it,' was their verdict.
Going back to the thread, what's also worth noticing is that the author didn't bring just one frame. They brought two, and that's what triggers the emotional response, the anxiety and confusion.

t: Great Business Leaders Love the Flywheel
q: A business is not a group of departments; it is a network of interdependencies. Sales promises what product has yet to deliver. The product roadmap gets impacted by what support hears during the last escalation.

A flywheel is heavy and slow at the start. Every push seems to accomplish nothing. Then the pushes begin to compound, and eventually momentum starts to build. The catch is that the pushes have to land in the same place.

Amazon's loop started with book selection and a great customer experience. A better experience brought more traffic. Traffic attracted third-party sellers. More sellers meant more selection, which improved the experience again.
No single move on that list is clever. A competitor could have copied any one of them. What was hard to copy was the loop because it only pays out when all parts of it are running.

In almost every business, one component is quietly throttling the rest, and it is rarely the one getting the most attention. Fix that part, and everything you have already built starts working harder.

q: One thing we know about professional learning, both from research and experience, is that one and done workshops or learning sessions do not move the needle in helping teachers apply their knowledge to the classroom. Educators must understand the why but also the how before we can apply our learning.

If school systems are serious about using Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) as a framework or umbrella for school reform, then schools need to spend time on the following areas: Developing Tier 1 First, Data Literacy Training, Intervention Protocols, Data-Based Decision Making.

Remember, no curriculum fits every setting all the time exactly as it was written. Can you be faithful to evidence-based and research-based practices while still having fidelity towards the curriculum?

Becoming data literate takes practice. Have you modeled data conversations while looking at school, grade-level, group, and student data? Do you have someone who could guide teacher teams through these discussions?

These steps mustn't be just part of a discussion, look good on paper, or produced into too many forms that schools are so good at developing. They must live in actionable steps that teams can come back to, analyze, discuss, and adjust. This is the very essence of the continuous improvement process.

t: Can You Care Too Much
q: I always thought empathy could never be excessive. Over recent months I've been forced to rethink my position and I've started questioning where empathy has a functional ceiling.
Eventually, without me realising, their mood became mine and I found it impossible to separate the two. That's when I had to be honest with myself about where I'd landed.
I'm a fixer, and always have been. My love language is action, meaning the way I express that I care for someone is doing something for them. The trouble is people don't behave like problems.

t: A Care-Giver's Trials
q: Annie Morgan wrapped her arms around her eldest daughter's waist and guided her toward the minivan, the two of them moving in a slow, sideways shuffle.
At 13, Ava was nearly as big as Annie, who stands just five feet flat, 110 pounds.

t: The Art of Delegation
q: Delegation is commonly understood as the distribution of work. Its harder and more consequential form is handing over authority, and the two are not the same thing.

Authority is different because it transfers the right to be wrong. To delegate a decision is to accept that it may be made differently from how the leader would have made it, and occasionally made badly, without the matter returning for correction.

The instinct to intervene is strongest precisely when intervention is most damaging, because a reasonable decision taken independently is often worth more to an organisation than a marginally better one that reinforces its dependence on a single person.

The organisations that outgrow their founders are not those whose leaders learned to distribute tasks more efficiently. They are those whose leaders learned to distribute the right to decide, and then, at the first uncomfortable test of that decision, declined to take it back.

t: The Consequences of More Words But Less Reading
q: Practically speaking, reading is the act of turning symbols on a page or screen into meaning in your head. And it happens in layers.

Research is clear that because skimming encourages people to jump from spot to spot and focus on keywords, it diminishes their ability to absorb and retain what's been written.

Many academics have argued that deep reading underlies our most important intellectual and emotional capacities, such as reasoning, inference, empathy, insight, perspective-taking, and critical analysis.

The most agreed-upon solution isn't to limit access to smartphones or to encourage people to skim less digitally, but rather to develop a "bi-literate" brain that can both scan fast and go deep with print-style reading.

Good leaders haven't given up on requiring team members to read. They build into team discussions a common reading set for everyone to digest and contemplate as preparation for robust debate on a topic, issue, or decision.

t: Precorrections
q: Precorrection is a quick, planned reminder of expected behaviour, delivered just before a moment you already know tends to go wrong. It is not a warning, or a rule on the wall, but a prompt timed to land right before the trouble spot.
When a student keeps making the same maths mistake, we don't just keep correcting it after the fact — we reteach the rule before they attempt the next problem.

Correction procedures are consequent manipulations designed to signal and stop inappropriate behavior after it occurs, while precorrection procedures are antecedent manipulations designed to prevent the occurrence of predictable inappropriate behavior.
A rehearsal can be as brief as asking a student to state what's expected, given in the minute before the target moment rather than earlier in the day.
The goal isn't a classroom full of reminders. It's a classroom where the moments that used to go wrong quietly stop needing them.

As the expected behaviour becomes the normal behaviour, the reminder should shrink — from a full sentence, to a gesture, to nothing at all. If you're still precorrecting the same moment six months from now, the pattern probably needs a different kind of attention.
Precorrection doesn't work in isolation. It sits in a healthy classroom culture made up of clear expectations, consistent routines, that are used deliberately.

t: On the Three Modes of Persuasion
q: Logos is the mode of persuasion that appeals to the intellect of its audience. A persuasive speech or essay that is logos heavy will rely largely on rational argumentation and be driven by data, syllogistic reasoning, and common sense argument.

Pathos is the mode of persuasion that appeals to the emotions of its audience. A persuasive speech or essay that is pathos heavy will rely largely on appeals to sympathy or anger or some other emotion.
It doesn't matter if you are right if you cannot persuade. It doesn't matter if you are a good person full of excellent knowledge if they don't trust or like you.
This well made point is why it is of critical importance for teachers of Rhetoric to not simply teach methods and modes, but to inculcate a love for what is true, good, and beautiful.

A good rhetor will not only refuse to lift a finger to persuade anyone into folly, but he will throw his whole person into the fight against it. A good rhetor desires truth for himself, wants to love and hate what he ought, is in pursuit of living the good life, and he wishes these things for his neighbor also.
Some have criticized rhetoric itself because of the abuses to which it can be put, but rhetoric doesn't abuse people, people abuse people.
But above all he must possess the quality which Cato places first and which is in the very nature of things the greatest and most important, that is, he must be a good man.

t: 1MW No. 318: Every Yes Has a Cost
q: By 2025, mobile orders were arriving faster than customers could get to the store. Baristas were trying to keep up with a stream of digital orders while also serving the customers standing directly in front of them.

There was nothing wrong with either idea. Convenience mattered, and connection mattered. The problem was trying to maximize both at the same time, through the same baristas, the same counters, and the same minutes.
Michael Porter calls this straddling: pursuing two different strategies without accepting the trade-offs required by either.
When people set their goals first, they tended to commit to more than their available time could realistically support. In effect, we give the same hour away more than once.
But when participants divided their available time before setting their goals, their goals became more realistic. They made more progress and were happier with the outcome.
Before saying yes to something new, ask: What will I have to say no to in order to say yes to this? If the answer is nothing, look again. Every yes costs something.

t: 1-to-1 Computer Initiatives: The Curious Case of Maine
q: 1-to-1 computer initiatives have one of the lowest effect sizes in the entire EdTech literature: approximately +0.12. That's less than one-third of the +0.42 benchmark commonly used to identify educational interventions with meaningful impact.

Between 1992 and 2002, Maine ranked among the nation's highest-performing education systems, with both fourth- and eighth-grade students consistently placing near the top of the country. Following the launch of MLTI, however, Maine's standing began a long-term decline.
By 2024, Maine had fallen from one of America's highest-performing education systems to roughly the middle of the pack in Grade 8, and the bottom quartile in Grade 4.
In 2017, 55% of Maine eighth-graders reported having access to a laptop in all classes, compared with just 15% in Massachusetts.

Unlike Maine, Massachusetts' national standing did not gradually erode over the next two decades: it strengthened. By 2002, Massachusetts had risen to the top of the nation in fourth-grade achievement - and by 2003, it had done the same in eighth grade.

Maine began this experiment as one of America's highest-performing education systems - but today, its eighth-graders sit roughly in the middle of the national pack, while its fourth-graders have fallen to the bottom quartile. After two decades, surely the burden of proof belongs with those still making the promises.

t: "Congrats! Now Go Talk to an Audience that Doesn't Want to Listen to You."
q: Every year we face SGO's, SGP's, walk-throughs, formal observations, action plans, and mountains of other paperwork, but students value our words much more than any of that stuff. I know this, because I experienced it when I was a student.
In high school, like many students, I lacked any sort of true self-confidence, I was constantly struggling to handle my emotions in a mature manner, and my social skills left a lot to be desired.

Mr. Romano had taught me three years earlier when I was a freshman, and I was sure he had forgotten me. In my mind, I was so insignificant that I was unworthy of note in his memory. But with a very brief interaction, Mr. Romano showed me I was wrong.
It's very possible Mr. Romano has completely forgotten our conversation, but I will remember it for the rest of my life.

Many educators in this room shared encouraging words with me when I was a struggling student teacher here ten years ago. Maybe you have forgotten about them, but I haven't. Your words make a difference. Always remember that.

This year you will be lucky enough to share in a student's joy, and a student will be lucky that they have someone like you to share in their sorrow. This year you will say something that a student will remember for the rest of their life.

t: You Still Can't Fix Culture. Change What Keeps Producing It.
q: Its argument was simple. Culture emerged from how the organisation actually worked. Values workshops, leadership speeches and change programmes played supporting roles. Daily organisational life did the real work.
Culture is the patterned residue of people acting through roles within an organisational system. That gives culture its diagnostic value.
Successful organisation? Study the culture. Failing organisation? Change the culture. Merger struggling? Integrate the cultures. Strategy stalled? Build a performance culture.
When everything became cultural, culture lost its explanatory value. It became an organisational Rorschach test.
An executive may be asked to act for the enterprise while being rewarded for protecting a function. A manager may carry accountability for an outcome while authority remains several levels above.

Culture becomes useful when we treat it as evidence. A pattern has appeared. People are behaving in recognisable ways.

q: The first is the complexity of the subject. A new prescription comes with complexity that's intrinsic to the task. You'll need to understand instructions, dosage, schedules, and refills.
Think of working memory as a truck that can carry a limited load. If the load is bigger than the capacity, things start to fall off. The same is true with the mind.

The problem is that chunking requires free working memory. If the mind is under pressure due to complexity, there aren't enough free resources for creating new chunks. So we read a dense scientific paper, but don't remember any of it.

In this example, the existing chunks of the nuclear physicist helped reduce the cognitive pressure and free up working memory. This is why what an audience already knows matters as much as what you're trying to teach them.
Intrinsic load: Complexity is all around us. This load represents how much processing is required to grasp the complexity of a subject, relative to the learner's existing knowledge.
The lesson: Manage the complexity of the subject you're communicating and make the presentation easier to consume.

A young man does not need a mentor to challenge his account of himself; he needs a comment section that agrees with him, and the algorithm is very good at finding him one.

t: The Disappearance of Memorization -- And What We Lost
q: In an 1854 lecture at the University of Lille, French inventor Louis Pasteur famously said, in the fields of observation, chance favors only the prepared mind. In other words, scientific breakthroughs depend on a scientist's prior knowledge.
Sadly, very few students today memorize anything other than the multiplication table. Even forty years ago, memorization was on its way out.

In The Knowledge Deficit, E.D. Hirsch writes, The systematic acquisition of broad knowledge is precisely what it takes to become a good reader. He goes on to laud factual knowledge as well as the language it entails.

education researcher Daniel Willingham explains, research from cognitive science has shown that the sorts of skills that teachers want for students -- such as the ability to analyze and to think critically -- require extensive factual knowledge.

We are, at our core, remembering and story-making creatures, says Wilfred McClay in his American history textbook, Land of Hope. He continues, A culture without memory will necessarily be barbarous and easily tyrannized, even if it is technologically advanced.
Schools should bring back memorization. Students deserve to have rich, beautiful, informative, and culturally important knowledge in their mind's permanent collection.

t: The Desire Beneath the Ambition August 11, 2026
q: They wanted space to consider who they were becoming. How they wanted to lead. How they could do meaningful work without allowing the work to consume them.

How do I actually have a positive impact on our deeply challenged communities? How do I do good in the world while also creating a life for my family, my partner, and myself that allows for presence, joy, and peace?

A kid from a highly educated family who decides to skip college and become an electrician is making a choice from a position of security; college was always available to them, and they are opting out of it.

t: Good Leaders Explain How Failure Will Be Judged Before It Happens https://admiredleadership.com/good-leaders-explain-how-failure-will-be-judged-before-it-happens/
q: What separates resilient teams from fragile ones is not whether failure happens, but whether people understand, in advance, how that failure will be evaluated.

When the criteria for judging failure only become visible after the fact, people reasonably conclude that the standard is arbitrary, or worse, that it will be applied punitively depending on politics or mood.
A team that has never been told how failure will be judged learns, from a single incident, exactly one data point about their leader's true standards. That is a dangerous way to build trust.
If you follow the agreed process, disclose problems immediately, and ask for help when you need it, a bad outcome will not define how I see you.

People stop hiding problems because they know concealment, not failure itself, is what will actually be punished. They start asking for help earlier because they know that asking is rewarded, not treated as an admission of weakness.

The paradox is that clarifying how failure will be judged, before it happens, is one of the most effective ways to reduce the frequency and severity of failure itself, because it makes the early warning signs of failure something people surface rather than hide.

t: Don't Just Prepare Them to Use It. Prepare Them to Change It.
q: We are preparing an entire generation of students to be highly competent users of tools that other people built, for purposes other people decided, with values other people encoded, and we are calling that preparation for the future.

If we only teach students to use AI tools well, we are training a generation of highly capable passengers.

t: Conflict Is Not the Problem, Silence Might Be

t: Back to School: Between the First and Last Day of Class
q: The single biggest challenge we face is one of meaning: how do I know that my work is meaningful, that it actually bears fruit? This is the quandary of every teacher (and parent), and what amplifies the difficulty is the reality that human beings are changeable.
The curriculum is not messianic. Throughout history, how many villains have studied the same great works of literature and philosophy, and yet rejected noble pursuits?
We cannot force people to be better. We can and should limit acting out and misbehavior, but we do not control the heart of another.

Our foundation, then, is rather simple: we trust in the efficacy of ordinary means. What I mean by this is that we believe if we educate students in the right way, it will make a difference for them and ultimately for society.
We don't prejudge our students, colleagues, or parents. We let their actions and words speak for themselves. When something makes us wonder, we ask about it.

The difference you will make cannot be measured today, or tomorrow, or even next year. In fact, I'm not sure it can ever be measured in exactly a way that would satisfy us; that would give us undeniable evidence of success.

t: AI can do lots of things... but should it?
q: I've been sitting with a distinction lately that I don't think gets made often enough in conversations about AI and learning: the gap between what AI can do and what it should do, given what we actually know about how people learn.
AI can generate a complete, polished essay outline in four seconds. Should a student who is still learning how to structure an argument receive that outline before attempting their own? Probably not.

A vendor can show you, in ninety seconds, that their tool can do something impressive. Almost no vendor demo includes should we be giving students this at this moment in their learning, because that question doesn't sell software.
Does providing this capability, right now, to this student, at this point in their learning, support or bypass the specific cognitive work this task is meant to build.
At that point the struggle has already happened, and the tool is adding value rather than removing necessary difficulty.

That is a judgment call about timing and sequencing that has to be made deliberately, task by task, student by student, and it is exactly the judgment call that gets skipped when the operating question is only can it do this.

t: Why Learn to Write in the Age of AI?
q: Schools often treat writing as the final step of learning: first you understand it, then you write it up. But in practice, writing is often the very thing that creates understanding.
So if a teenager asked me why they should bother to learn to write in the age of AI, I would tell them this: writing is thinking.

When you write about a topic from memory, you're forced to pull information out of your head rather than simply recognize it on a page. This kind of active retrieval strengthens memory significantly more than simply rereading or highlighting.

Psychologists have shown that most of us walk around with an "illusion of explanatory depth", which means that we feel like we understand things far better than we actually do, until we're asked to explain them.

Desirable difficulty, which describes conditions that slow learning down in the moment but make it stick far better in the long run, is the underlying idea behind all of these learning science concepts.

t: The War for the Human Soul: Five Lessons from C.S. Lewis's Space Trilogy
q: Lewis wrote the Space Trilogy between 1938 and 1945, in the middle of WWII, and it's quite impressive how he managed to predict so accurately what our very own postmodern ideological landscape would look like.

Masterfully, Lewis reminds us that our world is a fallen one, in which fighting will always be a necessity. This is an important reminder for us, because forgetting the truth of the earth as a battleground will make us more liable to fall into nihilism, despair, or pleasure-seeking.
The lesson for us then, is that discomfort, resistance, and cultural hostility are the expected conditions of a fallen world in which we've chosen to reject God.

t: The Truth About People Pleasing
q: The root of chronic people pleasing is not concern for others. It's concern for their acceptance and approval.

Psychologists find that what underlies people pleasing is the fear of being disliked and rejected. When we bend over backward to accommodate others at the expense of our own needs, it's because we depend on them for self-esteem.
Every time I failed to tell a driver that the car felt like Antarctica, I was setting another passenger up to shiver.
People pleasing is based on insecure attachment. We become people pleasers when we discover that others only value us when we're cooperative to the point of being submissive and deferential.
We shouldn't mistake the past origin of a behavior pattern for the current purpose it serves. A fear of being disliked leads too many of us to put our image above our values.
Sharing your preferences is not a display of disrespect. It's an expression of self-respect.

t: The Idea That Refused to Die: Part 1: From Bartlett to the Cognitive 'Revolution'
q: In his 1932 book Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology, Frederic Bartlett first introduced the notion of cognitive schemas (or schemata), a term he adapted from the work of his close friend and professional confidant Henry Head.

Rather than supporting the warehouse metaphor of memory, where static traces or images are stored in the brain, Bartlett's studies pointed towards a more complex and nuanced picture. His participants didn't recall the stimulus material exactly or within its entirety, but reconstructed the material.

If the brain uses biological schema to constantly track and adjust physical posture based on past movements, thought Bartlett, it must use a cognitive schema to track, adjust, and interpret new information and experiences based on past knowledge.
Despite this choice, Bartlett writes: 'I strongly dislike the term "schema". It is at once too definite and too sketchy' (page 201-202).
By 1932, Bartlett's ideas were becoming eclipsed by behaviourism. Behaviourism discouraged all that could not be directly observed.

Researchers at Cambridge never stopped studying mental processes; their emphasis just shifted. So when Bartlett published Thinking in 1958, it wasn't part of a cognitive revolution, but rather a continuation of what Cambridge had been doing all along.

t: The Divide Was Already There
q: AI didn't fracture the campus. It found the fractures. Whether it widens them or heals them is the most consequential choice higher education will make this decade.

At the University of Maryland, AI-related misconduct cases jumped 59% in a single year. In an Inside Higher Ed survey, 85% of students said they'd used generative AI for coursework in the past year -- one in five to write entire essays.
A University of Chicago study found something devastating this year: about 60% of students admit to using AI, but they estimate 90% of their peers do.

This is the reframe I want to offer: AI doesn't divide campuses. It audits them. It finds every place where trust was already thin, where work was already performative, where governance was already theater.
As of April 2026, 0.7% of students had completed the voluntary AI training. A systemwide survey of 94,000 people found 52% of faculty saying AI had negatively affected their teaching.

t: Retconning the Curriculum: Why the Science of Learning Has a Serious Design Problem
q: In the science of learning, the practice of retrieving previously learned material from memory is about the closest thing we have to penicillin in learning terms.

They have mutated from properties which exist to serve a curriculum into a range of techniques which give the impression of effective teaching but in reality, often grafted onto curricula never designed for them.

In 2020, Doug Rohrer and colleagues at the University of South Florida took several of the most used Maths textbooks in US schools and coded every problem (over 13,000 of them) against an ingenious question: does this practice problem require the student to retrieve anything from a previous chapter or does it just live inside the existing chapter?
For me, all this confirms the fact that the science of learning has far more to do with curriculum design than teaching activities.

A classroom full of kids raising mini-whiteboards like a Mexican wave might give the impression of learning but unless we examine closely what was being attended to then we risk the whole enterprise being pedagogical kayfabe.
To borrow again from Christine Counsell, retrieval practice without a destination or return path is an intransitive pedagogy, a pedagogy without an object.
The evidence never showed that quizzing strengthens memory per se; it showed that retrieval at a delay, timed against forgetting, strengthens memory.

Retconning the curriculum by bolting on the science of learning to materials that were never designed with them in mind might look evidence based but we will find out later if any learning actually took place, and probably too late.
